one_liner: Rust SIMD XML parser and XPath 1.0 engine using a flat structural index; beats pugixml on large, attribute-dense files.
what_it_does: A Rust crate, plus the `sxq` command-line tool, that turns XML bytes into a read-only structural index instead of a DOM, then runs XPath 1.0 queries against it. It supports all 13 axes and the full function set, and passes 327/327 libxml2 and 1015/1023 pugixml conformance tests. The API is `simdxml::parse(&[u8]) -> XmlIndex`, which borrows the input, with `xpath` / `xpath_text` / `eval`, a reusable `CompiledXPath`, batch helpers for many documents, query-driven lazy parsing (`parse_for_xpath`), and mmap-able `.sxi` sidecar indexes (`load_or_parse`). It does not replace pugixml: there is no node tree, no mutation or serialization, and no C/C++ API.
how_it_is_fast: Parsing follows simdjson's stage-1 idea: 64-byte blocks are compared against `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` with AVX2, SSE4.2 or NEON and packed into u64 bitmaps, and quoted regions are masked with a prefix-XOR (PMULL carry-less multiply on ARM, a shift-XOR chain on x86). That classifier only runs when a 4 KB sample shows more than 5 quotes per tag; otherwise a memchr-based scanner jumps from `<` to `<`. The output is a struct-of-arrays index of about 16 bytes per tag, against about 35 bytes per DOM node. XPath then runs on CSR child arrays, pre/post-order numbering (O(1) ancestor tests), posting lists of interned tag names, and fused descendant scans; the CSR arrays are built lazily, only for multi-step paths. Files are mmap'd, and in the CLI anything of 1 MB or more is split at `>`...`<` boundaries, parsed on all cores, and merged in one sequential pass.
when_to_use: Read-only XPath extraction from large, record-oriented dumps (hundreds of MB to multi-GB, e.g. DBLP or PubMed) on a multi-core machine. The author's blog puts the DBLP index at ~3.6 GB against ~7.9 GB for pugixml's DOM.

Attribute-dense XML such as SVG or flat attribute records. This is where the SIMD quote masking pays off: 1.7-2.6x over pugixml end-to-end and 4.0x over quick-xml parse-only on the project's 1 MB attribute-heavy file.
Shell pipelines that currently use `xmllint --xpath`. `sxq` is a jq-style CLI with count, raw, JSON and NUL-separated output, and the README reports it 6.4-17.5x faster than xmllint.

Querying the same big file repeatedly (a `.sxi` sidecar is reloaded by mmap, so there is no re-parse), or running one compiled query over thousands of small files (the batch API with a bloom-filter prescan).
Rust services, or Python/Elixir through the simdxml org's bindings, that need XPath 1.0 over trusted, well-formed UTF-8 input.
when_not_to_use: You need a DOM to edit or save, or pugixml's tree-navigation API. simdxml is a query-only index, and C++ callers would have to write their own FFI layer.

Untrusted, malformed or non-UTF-8 input. Upfront UTF-8 validation was removed for speed (commit 8a7fdd4), text is handed back through `from_utf8_unchecked`, and mismatched close tags are not detected (the `MismatchedCloseTag` error variant is never raised). DTDs are not processed, and only the five predefined entities and numeric entities are decoded.

Workloads dominated by `count()` / `contains()`, or small files. pugixml wins those PubMed queries (117 vs 133 ms, 148 vs 162 ms), and under 1 MB the README says all native tools are within startup noise.

XPath that depends on namespaces. `pfx:name` tests are matched against the literal tag text, with no prefix-to-URI resolution, so a document that uses a default namespace or a different prefix will not match.

Anything needing a maintained dependency. It has 14 stars and one main author; v0.1.0 through v0.2.1 all shipped on 26-27 March 2026 with no main-branch commits since, and a third-party fix for index corruption (PR #4) was withdrawn unmerged.

integration.dependencies: nom 7, thiserror 2, memchr 2, memmap2 0.9, xxhash-rust 0.8 (xxh3); the sxq CLI adds only memmap2
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX2 or SSE4.2 detected at runtime, scalar fallback); aarch64 NEON (selected at compile time, and uses PMULL without a feature check); other targets use a scalar/memchr path
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. `XmlIndex` is plain Vecs over a borrowed `&[u8]`, so the compiler auto-derives Send + Sync for it. `xpath()` / `xpath_text()` take `&self`, but `eval()` takes `&mut self` because it builds the CSR indexes lazily, so call `ensure_indices()` before sharing an index across threads. The library spawns its own scoped threads for `parse_parallel`, the batch APIs and CSR builds above 10K tags.

gotchas: Quote state in the SIMD two-stage path is tracked across the whole document, not per tag. A lone `"` or `'` in text content (e.g. `don't`) masks every later `<` and `>`, silently dropping the rest of the document from the index. This affects only files routed to that path (more than 5 quotes per tag in the first 4 KB). The fix, PR #4 from June 2026, was withdrawn unmerged; it also reports phantom tags from `<` inside comments or CDATA on that same path.
On aarch64, `neon.rs` calls `vmull_p64` (PMULL) with no `target_feature` gate or runtime check. Per PR #4, this traps with an illegal instruction on ARMv8 cores that lack the crypto extension.

Depth limits, from reading the source (not tested). The sequential scanner keeps parents in a fixed 32-entry stack, so tags nested deeper than 32 get no parent pointer and child/parent steps below that depth can miss. The parallel merge uses a 4096-entry stack with no bounds guard, so deeper nesting panics.

`sxq` automatically switches to all-core parallel parsing for files of 1 MB or more; pass `-t 1` for a single-threaded comparison. Its parallel splitter accepts any `>` followed by `<`, which can fall inside a CDATA section that contains markup. `string-length()` counts bytes, not characters.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Parshred (C++20, AGPL-3.0: DOM/SAX/pull APIs, XPath, namespaces, DTD validation, W3C conformance in CI) and libsimdxml (a C++23 library with the same flat-index-plus-XPath-1.0 design, 1.15-1.24x pugixml on parse) are the native C++ options, and Parshred is the one to use for untrusted or namespace-heavy XML. Pick simdxml when you are in Rust or want a permissively licensed CLI for multi-core XPath extraction over multi-GB record dumps.
verified_claims_summary: All figures are the project's own hyperfine timings of whole processes: `sxq` (release build with LTO, rustc version unstated) against a small pugixml XPath shim built with `c++ -O2` against the system pugixml (1.14 per the author's blog). On an M4 Max that gave 3.2 s vs 8.3 s on 5.1 GB DBLP `//article` and 130 vs 174 ms on 195 MB PubMed, and on a Ryzen 9 3950X 14.7 vs 38.8 ms on a 10 MB attribute-heavy file. However, sxq used every core and, on DBLP and PubMed, printed only a match count, while the single-threaded pugixml shim printed every match's text, and pugixml wins PubMed `count()` and `contains()` outright.
status_note: Listed as active, but every commit landed on 26-27 March 2026 (crates.io v0.1.0 through v0.2.1, about 5.7k downloads) and main has had nothing since. MIT OR Apache-2.0 is declared only in Cargo.toml and the README, with no LICENSE file, and it installs with `cargo add simdxml` or `cargo install simdxml-cli`.
